items.title: DeepSeek open-sources Super-agent prototype: a Router and Worker design for autonomous coding agents
items.original_title: 刚刚，DeepSeek重磅发布全新Agent架构：AI开始指挥AI干活
items.summary: DeepSeek's Harness team published 'Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System' and put an MIT-licensed reference prototype, dsh-superagent-prototype, on GitHub. A main router session handles human interaction, keeps global context and dispatches tickets; isolated worker sessions, each in its own directory, do the work in parallel and report back. Per the architecture doc the router has 14 application tools and workers 6, and workers cannot ask humans questions. The agent listens to GitHub, opens work items and replies with PRs. The README calls it a research prototype, not an official product.
items.why_it_matters: It shows how DeepSeek thinks about proactive multi-session coding agents on its open Harness, a design competing agent products will be compared against. It is an engineering exploration, not a model launch.

items.title: Nesformer compiles an NES CPU into the weights of a stock Qwen3.5 model
items.summary: A Show HN project compiles the NES 6502 CPU, its RAM and a cartridge ROM into a 466.6M-parameter Qwen3.5-architecture checkpoint with only 9.3M nonzero weights. The model predicts the CPU execution log token by token; the CPU matches the nestest golden log for 3,348 instructions and a 2,645,885-token full-game run matched exactly. It runs about 1,650 tokens/s on one core, 150-290x slower than a real NES, and supports only mapper-0 cartridges.
items.why_it_matters: A vivid demonstration that transformer weights can be compiled to emulate deterministic computation exactly, relevant to what LLM architectures can represent.

learn.title: Size a worker pool for a router: why latency explodes past utilisation 1
learn.why_today: DeepSeek's prototype has a router that dispatches tickets to isolated worker sessions, which makes the worker count a queueing-capacity question.
learn.explanation: Treat the router as a dispatcher feeding c workers, with triggers arriving at rate lambda and each task taking mean time s. Utilisation is rho = lambda*s/c. While rho < 1 the queue is stable and waits stay small; as rho approaches 1 waits blow up, and above 1 they grow without bound. The simulation below uses illustrative numbers only (3-minute tasks, Poisson arrivals): 4 workers cope with 1 trigger/min (rho 0.75) but collapse at 5/min, while 16 workers cope with 5/min (rho 0.94, p95 wait about 5 minutes) but not 10/min. Batching or deduplicating triggers lowers lambda; adding workers raises c. It breaks when tasks are not exchangeable, e.g. long tasks blocking a worker or tasks with dependencies.

learn.title: Emulate a CPU as a next-state table, and see what memorising misses
learn.why_today: Nesformer has a model predict a CPU's execution log one token at a time; this exercise writes the same idea by hand at toy scale.
learn.explanation: A deterministic machine is a function from state to next state, so its execution log is a sequence a next-token predictor can reproduce exactly. Below, a four-instruction accumulator CPU generates a golden log, and a dictionary 'model' memorises state to next-state pairs from it. Replay matches exactly, which is the nestest-style check. But a different program (LDI 6) visits states the table never saw, so it fails: exact emulation requires encoding the transition rule, not just the observed transitions. Toy CPU and table are illustrative and say nothing about how nesformer's weights are constructed.
learn.python:
# Tiny accumulator CPU whose execution log is a token stream.
PROG = [("LDI",5),("ADD",3),("SUB",1),("JNZ",1),("HLT",0)]
def step(s):
    pc,a,z = s; op,x = PROG[pc]
    if op=="LDI": a=x
    elif op=="ADD": a=(a+x)&255
    elif op=="SUB": a=(a-x)&255
    pc = x if (op=="JNZ" and a!=0) else pc+1
    z = int(a==0)
    return (pc,a,z)
def run(n):
    s=(0,0,0); log=[s]
    while PROG[s[0]][0]!="HLT" and len(log)<n:
        s=step(s); log.append(s)
    return log
golden = run(40)
# "Model" = a lookup table learned from the golden log: state -> next state
table = {a:b for a,b in zip(golden, golden[1:])}
state, out = golden[0], [golden[0]]
while state in table and len(out)<len(golden):
    state = table[state]; out.append(state)
print(len(golden), "steps; replay matches golden:", out==golden)
print("distinct transitions:", len(table))
PROG[0] = ("LDI", 6)   # new program: the memorised table has never seen these states
new = run(40)
print("unseen transitions in new run:", sum(1 for a in new[:-1] if a not in table))
